objectives: Trace the transition from late antiquity to the medieval world systems.
Survey the Islamic golden age + Tang-Song China + medieval Europe.
Analyze the early-modern transformations — Mongols, Black Death, Renaissance, Reformation, Columbian exchange, Atlantic slavery, early capitalism.

slides.title: Late antiquity to medieval: Byzantium, Islam, Tang-Song, feudal Europe
slides.body:
**Late antiquity** (c. 250-750 CE): the long transition between the classical and medieval worlds. Peter Brown's *The World of Late Antiquity* (1971) reshaped the period — not a 'decline' but a transformation. Major dynamics: Christianization of the Roman world, barbarian settlements + new kingdoms, the rise of Islam, monasticism, urban contraction in the west + persistence in the east.

**Fall of the Western Roman Empire** (5th c CE):
- 410 CE Visigoths sack Rome; 476 CE Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus.
- New 'barbarian' kingdoms: Visigoths (Spain), Ostrogoths + Lombards (Italy), Franks (Gaul), Anglo-Saxons (Britain), Vandals (North Africa).
- Gibbon's *Decline and Fall* (1776-89) gave the period its dominant frame; Pirenne (*Mahomet et Charlemagne* 1937) argued the real break was the 7th-c Islamic conquests; Peter Brown + Bryan Ward-Perkins debate continues.

**Byzantine Empire** (330-1453): the Eastern Roman state.
- Capital **Constantinople** (founded by Constantine 330 CE).
- **Justinian I** (r. 527-565 CE): codified Roman law as the *Corpus Juris Civilis* (533-534; Digest + Code + Institutes + Novels) — the basis of European civil law to this day. Reconquered parts of the west (North Africa, Italy, southern Spain). Built **Hagia Sophia** (532-537 CE).
- Survived plague of Justinian (541-549, first historical bubonic outbreak), Arab conquests (lost Syria + Egypt 634-642), iconoclasm controversy (8th-9th c), Macedonian renaissance (9th-11th c), schism with Rome (1054).
- Final fall 1453 (Mehmed II, Ottoman conquest).

**Islamic golden age** (c. 750-1258, peaking under the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad):
- **Muhammad** (c. 570-632 CE); Qur'an revealed 610-632; Hijra 622 CE (year 1 AH).
- **Rashidun caliphate** (632-661) + **Umayyad** (661-750, Damascus) + **Abbasid** (750-1258, Baghdad — founded 762).
- **Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom)** in Baghdad: translation movement (Syriac + Greek + Persian + Sanskrit → Arabic) under Harun al-Rashid + Al-Ma'mun (early 9th c). Preserved + extended classical Greek learning.
- **Al-Khwarizmi** (c. 780-850): *Kitab al-Jabr* (c. 820) gave us 'algebra' + Hindu-Arabic numerals to the West + 'algorithm' (from his name).
- **Avicenna (Ibn Sina, 980-1037)**: *Canon of Medicine* + Aristotelian philosophy; medical textbook in Europe to 17th c.
- **Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126-1198, Córdoba)**: commentaries on Aristotle; major influence on Latin scholasticism (Thomas Aquinas).
- Algebra, trigonometry, optics (Alhazen / Ibn al-Haytham *Book of Optics* c. 1011-1021), astronomy, medicine, chemistry; preserved + transmitted Greek classics to medieval Europe.
- Cordoba caliphate (756-1031) in al-Andalus + Cairo's Fatimid caliphate (909-1171) were parallel poles.

**Tang (618-907) + Song (960-1279) China**:
- **Tang**: cosmopolitan empire; Chang'an (modern Xi'an) the world's largest city ~1 million; civil-service examination system; Buddhism flourishes (though periodically suppressed); poetry (Li Bai, Du Fu); woodblock printing.
- **Song** (Northern 960-1127; Southern 1127-1279): commercial + technological revolution. Movable-type printing (Bi Sheng c. 1040), gunpowder, compass, paper money (jiaozi), advanced metallurgy + shipbuilding (Joseph Needham documented at length). Neo-Confucianism (Zhu Xi 1130-1200).
- Per-capita GDP estimates (Maddison) place Song China at or above contemporary Europe.

**Heian Japan** (794-1185): aristocratic culture; *Tale of Genji* (Murasaki Shikibu, c. 1000-1012) — often called the world's first novel; Pure Land + Tendai Buddhism; transition to feudal Kamakura shogunate (1185).

**Medieval European feudalism** (c. 800-1300):
- **Carolingian** revival (Charlemagne crowned Emperor 800 CE); Carolingian renaissance + manuscript culture.
- **Feudal contract**: lord-vassal personal bond + fief; manorial economy with serfs; the 'feudal pyramid' (king → nobles → knights → peasants) is a simplification critiqued by historians (Susan Reynolds *Fiefs and Vassals* 1994).
- **High medieval revival** (c. 1000-1300): population doubles; clearing forests + draining marshes (*Drang nach Osten*); urban revival (Italian communes — Venice, Florence, Genoa; Hanseatic League in the north).
- **Crusades** (1096-1291): Latin Christendom + Levant; First Crusade took Jerusalem 1099; Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople 1204.
- **Universities** founded: Bologna (1088), Paris (1150), Oxford (1167), Cambridge (1209), Salamanca (1218). Scholasticism (Anselm, Abelard, Aquinas).
- **Gothic architecture** + cathedrals (St-Denis 1144, Chartres, Notre-Dame de Paris).
- **Magna Carta** (1215, Runnymede): foundational charter limiting royal power.

slides.title: Crisis + transformation: Mongols, Black Death, Ming, Ottoman, Mughal
slides.body:
**Mongol Empire** (1206-c. 1368): largest contiguous empire in history.
- **Genghis Khan (Temüjin)** (c. 1162-1227) unified the steppe tribes 1206; conquered Khwarazm (1219-1221), northern China (Jin 1234 under Ögedei).
- By 1279 the Mongols ruled from the Pacific to the Black Sea + Mediterranean — c. 24 million km², ~110 million subjects.
- **Successor khanates**: Yuan (China — Kublai Khan, *r. 1260-1294*), Chagatai (Central Asia), Ilkhanate (Persia + Iraq), Golden Horde (Russia + steppe). Marco Polo's travels (c. 1271-1295).
- **Pax Mongolica**: trans-Eurasian trade + travel + cultural exchange — gunpowder, printing, the compass, paper, plague all travel.
- **Consequences**: destruction (Baghdad sacked 1258 ended the Abbasid caliphate); cosmopolitan transmission; established Eurasian frame.

**The Black Death** (1347-1351 in the Mediterranean + Europe; recurring waves to 18th c):
- Yersinia pestis (bubonic + pneumonic plague), likely originating in Central Asia, spread via Mongol-era trade routes to the Crimea + then by Genoese galleys to Sicily (1347), Italy + France (1348), England (1348-49), Scandinavia, Russia.
- Mortality: 30-60% of European population (William Naphy + Andrew Spicer; Ole Benedictow estimates higher); some places ~80%; the Mamluk + Mongol + Ming worlds also devastated.
- Demographic + economic consequences: labor shortages → rising wages + serfdom's gradual collapse in western Europe (Postan-Hatcher debate); peasant revolts (Jacquerie 1358, English Peasants' Revolt 1381); shift in cultural orientation (*danse macabre*, *memento mori*).
- Pomeranz + Pamuk + Voigtländer + Voth on the **Black Death + Great Divergence**: the labor scarcity may have shifted European agriculture toward capital-intensive + commercial forms, with long-term divergence implications (debated; see lesson 5).

**Ottoman Empire** (c. 1299-1922):
- Origin in late 13th-c Anatolia (Osman I); expansion into Byzantium + Balkans.
- **Mehmed II 'the Conqueror'** took Constantinople 1453 (end of Byzantium).
- **Süleyman the Magnificent** (r. 1520-1566): peak — Anatolia, Levant, Egypt, North Africa, southeastern Europe to Hungary; siege of Vienna 1529. Multiethnic + multireligious (millet system).
- Long decline traditionally dated from 1683 (failed Vienna siege) to 1922.

**Ming dynasty** (1368-1644): Han Chinese restoration after Mongol Yuan.
- **Hongwu Emperor** founder (r. 1368-1398); moved capital to Beijing under Yongle (r. 1402-1424).
- **Zheng He's voyages** (1405-1433): seven expeditions to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, East Africa with treasure fleets of 200+ ships, dwarfing contemporary European vessels. Discontinued by the Ming bureaucracy — a famous counterfactual node (Diamond, Pomeranz). The Great Wall (in its current Ming form) constructed.
- Late Ming commercial + cultural florescence; collapse 1644 to the **Qing** (Manchu, 1644-1912).

**Mughal Empire** (1526-1857, peak 1605-1707):
- **Babur** (descended from Timur + Genghis) defeated Lodi sultans (1526).
- **Akbar the Great** (r. 1556-1605): religious tolerance, *Din-i-Ilahi* synthesis, integrated Hindu rajputs.
- **Shah Jahan** (r. 1628-1658): Taj Mahal.
- **Aurangzeb** (r. 1658-1707): peak extent; intolerance + over-extension; subsequent decline opened the way to Maratha resurgence + British East India Company.

**Renaissance** (c. 1350-1600, Italy radiating outward):
- **Petrarch** (1304-1374) + classical humanism; **Boccaccio** *Decameron* (c. 1353).
- Florence under Medici (15th c); civic humanism (Bruni); **Leonardo da Vinci** (1452-1519); **Michelangelo** (1475-1564); **Raphael** (1483-1520).
- **Machiavelli** *The Prince* (1513, printed 1532).
- **Northern Renaissance**: Erasmus (*In Praise of Folly* 1511), More (*Utopia* 1516), Dürer, Holbein.
- Printing — **Gutenberg's** movable type c. 1440-1455; **Eisenstein** *The Printing Press as an Agent of Change* (1979) — Europe's information revolution.

slides.title: Reformation, Scientific Revolution, Columbian exchange, Atlantic slavery, early capitalism
slides.body:
**Protestant Reformation** (1517-1648):
- **Martin Luther** (1483-1546) posted 95 Theses at Wittenberg on October 31, 1517, attacking indulgences. Translated the New Testament into German (1522). Justification by faith alone (*sola fide*) + scripture alone (*sola scriptura*).
- **Huldrych Zwingli** (Zurich), **John Calvin** (1509-1564, Geneva — *Institutes of the Christian Religion* 1536/1559).
- **English Reformation**: Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy (1534); Anglican settlement under Elizabeth I.
- **Counter-Reformation / Catholic Reformation**: Council of Trent (1545-1563), Jesuits (founded 1540 by Ignatius Loyola), Baroque art, Roman Inquisition.
- **Wars of religion**: French wars (1562-1598, St. Bartholomew's Day massacre 1572); Eighty Years' War (1568-1648); Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) — ended with Peace of Westphalia, foundational for the modern state system.
- **Weber** *The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism* (1905): controversial thesis linking Calvinist asceticism to capitalist mentality.

**Scientific Revolution** (c. 1543-1687):
- **Copernicus** *De revolutionibus orbium coelestium* (1543): heliocentrism.
- **Tycho Brahe** (1546-1601) precise observations; **Kepler** (1571-1630) three laws (1609, 1619); **Galileo** (1564-1642) telescope + dynamics (*Sidereus Nuncius* 1610; condemned 1633).
- **Descartes** *Discourse on Method* (1637); **Boyle** + the Royal Society (1660); **Newton** *Principia* (1687).
- Historiography: Koyré, Kuhn (*Structure of Scientific Revolutions* 1962 — lesson 6), Shapin + Schaffer (*Leviathan and the Air-Pump* 1985 — lesson 6).

**Columbian exchange + early-modern globalization** (1492-1800):
- **Columbus** 1492; the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided the world between Portugal + Castile.
- **Alfred W. Crosby** *The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492* (1972) + *Ecological Imperialism* (1986) — see lesson 7. The exchange of plants, animals, microbes, peoples reshaped both hemispheres.
- New World → Old World: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cassava, cacao, tobacco, chili, beans, squash, sweet potato. Old → New: wheat, rice, sugar, coffee, citrus, horses, cattle, pigs, sheep + diseases — smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus — devastating Native populations (50-90% mortality across the Americas; Charles Mann *1491*).
- **Silver from Potosí + Zacatecas** flowed into Ming + Qing China via Manila galleons (Andre Gunder Frank *ReOrient* 1998; Flynn + Giráldez 'born with a silver spoon' 1995).

**Atlantic slavery + the triangular trade** (c. 1500-1888):
- ~12.5 million Africans embarked, ~10.7 million arrived (Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database; David Eltis + David Richardson).
- Sugar (Caribbean, Brazil) + tobacco (Chesapeake) + rice (Carolina) + cotton (US South — see lesson 5) plantation complexes.
- **Eric Williams** *Capitalism and Slavery* (1944): slavery + Atlantic trade financed British industrialization (the 'Williams thesis' — still debated; Engerman; more recently Joseph Inikori, Sven Beckert).
- **Walter Rodney** *How Europe Underdeveloped Africa* (1972) — see lesson 5.
- Abolition: Saint-Domingue / Haitian Revolution (1791-1804 — Toussaint Louverture, Dessalines, C.L.R. James *Black Jacobins* 1938); British abolition (1807 trade; 1834 emancipation); US Civil War (1861-65); Brazil last in 1888.

**Early modern capitalism** (Braudel *Civilization and Capitalism* 1979; Wallerstein 1974):
- Joint-stock companies — Dutch VOC (1602), English EIC (1600), Hudson's Bay (1670).
- Amsterdam Bourse (1602), Bank of Amsterdam (1609), Bank of England (1694).
- **Tulip mania** (1636-37, Mackay 1841 — debated, see Goldgar *Tulipmania* 2007).
- Mercantilist state policy: navigation acts, monopolies, bullionism.
- Braudel's three-tier model: market exchange (transparent) → market economy (regional integration) → capitalism (the 'shadow zone' of monopoly + speculation + state-finance entanglement).

By 1750 the world was decisively connected: Atlantic system, Indian Ocean trade, Manila galleons, Russian Pacific frontier, Cape Colony. The **Great Divergence** (Pomeranz 2000 — lesson 5) — Europe's industrial leap-ahead — emerges from this connected world, not in isolation.

question.question: Trace the consequences of the Black Death (1347-51)
question.goal: How did the Black Death reshape Europe's society + economy + culture?

steps.prompt: Demographic shock: what was the immediate effect?

acceptedAnswers: 30-60% mortality; population took ~150-200 years to recover

steps.reveal: 30-60% of European population died in 1347-51, with recurring waves to the 18th century. Pre-plague European population ~75-80 million; bottomed at ~40-50 million ~1400; full recovery only by ~1550. Comparable mortality across the Mediterranean + Middle East. Mongol + Ming worlds also struck. The most lethal demographic event in European history before the 20th c.

steps.prompt: Economic consequence: what changed in the labor market?

acceptedAnswers: labor scarcity → rising wages + decline of serfdom in western Europe

steps.reveal: Sharp labor scarcity → rising real wages (perhaps 50-100% by mid-1400s; Phelps Brown + Hopkins wage series); peasants could leave manors + bargain; serfdom's enforcement weakened in western Europe (already weakening in some regions). In eastern Europe the opposite happened — the 'second serfdom' tightened bonded labor as landlords reasserted control (Brenner debate). Postan-Hatcher demographic explanation has been contested by Marxists (Brenner) — class structure, not just demography, mattered.

acceptedAnswers: peasant revolts; weakening of the church; shift in land tenure

hints: What followed in the next generation?
steps.reveal: Peasant revolts: Jacquerie (France 1358), English Peasants' Revolt (1381 — Wat Tyler, John Ball), Ciompi (Florence 1378), German peasants' wars (later, 1524-25). The Church's failure to explain or prevent the plague + the deaths of many clergy weakened its prestige (a pre-Reformation undermining). Land tenure: more land + fewer workers shifted bargaining power; in some places consolidation, in others peasant ownership. Pomeranz + Voigtländer + Voth argue this set up Europe's later commercial + capital-intensive trajectory.

acceptedAnswers: memento mori art + literature; eventual Renaissance + Reformation context

steps.reveal: Cultural: *danse macabre*, *memento mori*, the *Triumph of Death* — death as ubiquitous artistic theme. Boccaccio's *Decameron* (c. 1353) frames stories told by Florentines fleeing the plague. Religious life: flagellant movements, mysticism, lay piety (Brethren of the Common Life, Modern Devotion), antisemitic pogroms (Jews blamed; Strasbourg 1349, etc.). Long-term: the demographic + economic shock is one of multiple causes that connect to Italian Renaissance commerce + Reformation grievance + early modern capitalism — though historians are careful not to make Black Death do all the explanatory work (multi-causal, longue durée).

question.question: Why is the Islamic golden age (c. 750-1258, peaking under the Abbasid Caliphate) a pivotal episode in world intellectual history?
options: The Abbasid translation movement (Baghdad's Bayt al-Hikma / House of Wisdom under Harun al-Rashid + Al-Ma'mun, early 9th c) systematically rendered Greek, Syriac, Persian, + Sanskrit texts into Arabic — preserving + extending classical learning that Latin Europe had largely lost. Al-Khwarizmi's *Kitab al-Jabr* (c. 820) gave us algebra + Hindu-Arabic numerals + the word 'algorithm' (from his name). Avicenna (Ibn Sina, 980-1037, *Canon of Medicine*) + Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126-1198, Aristotle commentaries) influenced Latin scholasticism — Thomas Aquinas read Averroes via translations from Toledo. Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham, c. 965-1040) reshaped optics. Persian + Arabic poetry + Sufi mysticism (Rumi, Ibn Arabi) flourished. The 12th-13th century translations from Arabic into Latin (Toledo + Sicily) reopened Aristotle + Greek mathematics to Europe — directly enabling the European medieval revival + later Renaissance + Scientific Revolution. The Islamic world was the connective tissue of premodern Eurasian learning.
question.explanation: The Abbasid House of Wisdom translated Greek + Syriac + Persian + Sanskrit into Arabic, preserving classical learning. Al-Khwarizmi (algebra + algorithm), Avicenna (*Canon of Medicine*), Averroes (Aristotle commentaries), Alhazen (optics). 12th-c translations from Arabic into Latin (Toledo, Sicily) reopened Greek learning to Latin Europe — enabling later medieval + Renaissance + Scientific Revolution.

hints: House of Wisdom + Al-Khwarizmi + Avicenna + Averroes.
slides.workedSolution: House of Wisdom (Baghdad, early 9th c) translated Greek + Syriac + Persian + Sanskrit into Arabic. Al-Khwarizmi (algebra + Hindu-Arabic numerals + 'algorithm'), Avicenna (*Canon of Medicine*), Averroes (Aristotle), Alhazen (optics). 12th-c Latin translations from Arabic (Toledo + Sicily) reopened Greek learning to Europe — enabling later medieval + Renaissance + Scientific Revolution. Islamic world was the connective tissue of premodern Eurasian learning.

question.question: The 1492 'Columbian moment'
question.prompt: An undergraduate proposes a senior thesis titled 'How Columbus's voyage changed the world'. Drawing on Alfred Crosby's *Columbian Exchange* (1972) + *Ecological Imperialism* (1986), Charles Mann's *1491* + *1493*, and global + economic history, advise the student on how to reframe + scope the project. Address: (1) why the 'Columbus changed the world' framing is misleading without the Indian-Ocean + Pacific contexts (Pomeranz, Frank, Subrahmanyam — see lessons 5 + 7), (2) which biological + epidemiological + ecological mechanisms drove the exchange's consequences, (3) the role of silver from Potosí + Manila galleons in connecting the world economy to Ming + Qing China, (4) the moral + historiographical hazards of celebrating versus condemning 1492, and (5) what a properly comparative + connected-history version of the project looks like.

question.question: Pre-plague European population is estimated at $\sim 80$ million in 1347. If mortality was $40\%$ over 1347-51, what is the post-plague population (in millions, to nearest million)?
question.hint: $80 \times (1 - 0.40) = 80 \times 0.60 = 48$ million. Recovery to pre-plague levels took ~150-200 years — by ~1550. The labor scarcity reshaped wages + tenure + the structure of European agriculture (cf. Postan-Hatcher demographic model + Brenner debate).

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, explain how the medieval + early-modern world was shaped by the interplay of Islamic, Chinese, + European civilizations + the transformations of the 14th-17th centuries.
question.rubric: Mentions: late antiquity saw the rise of Byzantium (Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis), Islam (Muhammad 622; Abbasid House of Wisdom + Al-Khwarizmi + Avicenna + Averroes), + Tang-Song China (printing, gunpowder, compass, paper money — Song was the most advanced economy of its time). Medieval Europe revived after 1000 with universities, Gothic cathedrals, + commercial communes. The Mongol conquests (1206-c.1368) unified Eurasia + enabled the Black Death (1347-51, ~40% mortality), which reshaped labor + tenure + culture. Ming China's Zheng He voyages (1405-33), the Ottoman + Mughal empires, + the Renaissance + Reformation (Luther 1517) + Scientific Revolution (Copernicus 1543 → Newton 1687) followed. The Columbian exchange (Crosby 1972) + Atlantic slavery + early capitalism (Braudel) connected the world. Concludes: the medieval + early-modern centuries built the connected, contested world of the modern era.
